title: Life Processes
summary: Chapter 5 of Class 10 Science focuses on 'Periodic Classification of Elements'. This chapter explores the historical development of the periodic table, from Dobereiner's triads to Mendeleev's periodic table and finally to the modern periodic table. It discusses how elements are classified based on their atomic number and electron configuration, explaining the significance of groups and periods. The chapter highlights trends in atomic size, valency, metallic character, and chemical reactivity across periods and down groups. Understanding these periodic trends helps in predicting the properties of elements and their compounds, forming the foundation for advanced chemistry concepts.

sections.heading: Early Attempts at Classification
sections.para: Before the development of the modern periodic table, scientists attempted to classify elements based on their atomic weights and properties. Dobereiner observed that some elements could be grouped into triads where the atomic weight of the middle element was approximately the average of the other two. For example, calcium (atomic weight 40) is the average of lithium (7) and potassium (39). Newlands proposed the Law of Octaves, stating that every eighth element had similar properties when arranged in increasing order of atomic weights. However, this worked well only for lighter elements and failed beyond calcium. These early attempts laid the groundwork for more systematic classification.
points: Dobereiner's triads were groups of three elements with similar properties where the middle element had atomic weight nearly equal to the average of the other two
Newlands' Law of Octaves suggested that every eighth element exhibited similar properties when elements were arranged in increasing order of atomic weights
Both classification systems had limitations and could not accommodate all elements discovered at the time
These early attempts were important as they recognized patterns in elemental properties
Mendeleev later built upon these observations to create a more comprehensive periodic table
The limitations of these early systems highlighted the need for a better classification method

keyTerms.meaning: Groups of three elements with similar properties where the middle element's atomic weight was approximately the average of the other two
Newlands' observation that every eighth element had similar properties when arranged in increasing order of atomic weights
The average mass of atoms of an element, weighted according to the abundance of each isotope
The arrangement of elements based on their properties in a systematic manner

sections.trick: Remember Dobereiner's triads with 'LCP' (Lithium, Calcium, Potassium) - Calcium is the average of Lithium and Potassium.
sections.examPointer: CBSE frequently asks questions on Dobereiner's triads and Newlands' Law of Octaves, usually for 1-2 marks. Questions may ask you to identify triads or explain limitations of these early classification systems.

sections.heading: Mendeleev's Periodic Table
sections.para: Dmitri Mendeleev arranged elements in increasing order of atomic weights and grouped them with similar properties. His periodic table had horizontal periods and vertical groups. Mendeleev left gaps for undiscovered elements and even predicted their properties with remarkable accuracy. For example, he predicted the existence of eka-aluminium (later named gallium), eka-boron (scandium), and eka-silicon (germanium) with their properties. He also corrected the atomic weights of some elements, believing that atomic weight should be secondary to chemical properties. When noble gases were discovered, they were accommodated in a new group without disturbing the existing order. Mendeleev's periodic table was a significant advancement, though it had some limitations like anomalies in atomic weights and inability to explain the position of isotopes.
points: Mendeleev arranged elements in order of increasing atomic weights and grouped them with similar properties
He left gaps for undiscovered elements and predicted their properties accurately
He corrected atomic weights of some elements to maintain periodicity
When noble gases were discovered, they were placed in a separate group without disturbing the existing order
His periodic table helped in correcting atomic weights of certain elements
Mendeleev even predicted the existence and properties of elements like gallium, scandium, and germanium

keyTerms.meaning: A horizontal row in the periodic table containing elements with the same number of electron shells
A vertical column in the periodic table containing elements with similar chemical properties
Elements predicted by Mendeleev that were undiscovered at the time, named with prefix 'eka'
Mendeleev's version stated that the properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic weights

sections.trick: Remember Mendeleev's predictions with 'GSG' - Gallium (eka-aluminum), Scandium (eka-boron), Germanium (eka-silicon) - his three famous predictions.
sections.examPointer: Questions on Mendeleev's periodic table are common for 2-3 marks. You may be asked to explain his contributions, discuss limitations, or match predicted elements with their properties.

sections.heading: Modern Periodic Table
sections.para: The modern periodic table is based on Henry Moseley's work who showed that atomic number, not atomic weight, is the fundamental property governing periodicity. The modern periodic law states that 'the properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers.' Elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic numbers in periods and groups. The table has 18 groups and 7 periods. The position of an element in the periodic table determines its electron configuration, which in turn determines its chemical properties. The modern table overcame the limitations of Mendeleev's table by placing isotopes in the same position and explaining the anomalous positions of some elements. The table is divided into s, p, d, and f blocks based on the subshell that contains the last electron.
points: The modern periodic table is based on atomic number rather than atomic weight
Modern periodic law states that properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers
The table has 18 groups and 7 periods, with elements arranged in order of increasing atomic numbers
Elements are classified into s, p, d, and f blocks based on the subshell containing the last electron
The modern table resolved anomalies present in Mendeleev's periodic table
Isotopes are placed in the same position in the modern periodic table as they have the same atomic number

keyTerms.meaning: The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom, which determines its position in the periodic table
The properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers
Elements whose last electron enters the s-orbital, comprising groups 1 and 2
Elements whose last electron enters the p-orbital, comprising groups 13 to 18

sections.trick: Remember the blocks with 'SPDF' - S-block (groups 1-2), P-block (groups 13-18), D-block (groups 3-12), F-block (lanthanides and actinides).
sections.examPointer: Questions on the modern periodic table are common for 2-4 marks. You may be asked to explain the modern periodic law, identify blocks, or discuss advantages over Mendeleev's table.

sections.heading: Trends in the Periodic Table
sections.para: Several important trends can be observed in the periodic table. Atomic size decreases across a period from left to right due to increasing nuclear charge pulling electrons closer. It increases down a group as new electron shells are added. Valency first increases from 1 to 4 in the second period and then decreases to zero in noble gases. Metallic character decreases across a period and increases down a group. Non-metallic character shows the opposite trend. Electronegativity increases across a period and decreases down a group. Ionization energy generally increases across a period and decreases down a group. These trends help in predicting the chemical behavior of elements and their compounds.
points: Atomic size decreases across a period due to increasing nuclear charge and increases down a group due to addition of new electron shells
Valency increases from 1 to 4 in the second period and then decreases to zero in noble gases
Metallic character decreases across a period and increases down a group
Non-metallic character increases across a period and decreases down a group
Electronegativity increases across a period and decreases down a group
Ionization energy generally increases across a period and decreases down a group

The tendency of an element to lose electrons and form positive ions

sections.examPointer: Trends are frequently asked for 3-5 marks. Questions may ask you to explain trends with examples, compare elements across periods or down groups, or predict properties based on position in the table.

sections.heading: Periodic Properties - Atomic Size
sections.para: Atomic size or atomic radius is an important periodic property. It is defined as the distance from the center of the nucleus to the outermost shell of an atom. Atomic size decreases across a period from left to right because the nuclear charge increases, pulling the electrons closer to the nucleus. The addition of electrons occurs in the same shell, so the increased nuclear charge is not effectively shielded. Atomic size increases down a group because each successive element has an additional electron shell, which increases the distance between the nucleus and the outermost electrons. For example, in period 2, lithium has the largest atomic size and neon the smallest. In group 1, lithium has the smallest atomic size and cesium the largest.
points: Atomic size is the distance from the center of the nucleus to the outermost shell of an atom
Atomic size decreases across a period due to increasing nuclear charge with electrons added in the same shell
Atomic size increases down a group due to addition of new electron shells
The decrease in atomic size across a period is more pronounced in periods with smaller elements
The increase in atomic size down a group is less regular due to poor shielding effect of d and f electrons
Atomic size affects other properties like ionization energy and electronegativity

keyTerms.meaning: The distance from the center of the nucleus to the outermost shell of an atom
The positive charge of the nucleus due to protons, which attracts electrons
The reduction of the effective nuclear charge on an electron due to other electrons between it and the nucleus
Half the distance between the nuclei of two identical atoms joined by a covalent bond

sections.trick: Remember atomic size trend with 'L to R shrinks, T to B grows' - Left to Right across a period, atoms get smaller; Top to Bottom down a group, atoms get larger.
sections.examPointer: Questions on atomic size are common for 2-3 marks. You may be asked to explain the trend, compare atomic sizes of given elements, or explain exceptions to the trend.

sections.heading: Periodic Properties - Valency
sections.para: Valency is the combining capacity of an element and is determined by the number of valence electrons. In the periodic table, valency shows a periodic pattern. In a period, valency increases from 1 to 4 as we move from left to right, then decreases to zero in noble gases. For example, in period 2, lithium has valency 1, beryllium 2, boron 3, carbon 4, nitrogen 3, oxygen 2, fluorine 1, and neon 0. Down a group, valency generally remains the same for elements in the same group. For example, all alkali metals in group 1 have valency 1. However, there are exceptions, especially in transition metals where variable valency is common. The valency of an element is related to its position in the periodic table and helps in predicting its chemical behavior and compound formation.
points: Valency is the combining capacity of an element, determined by the number of valence electrons
In a period, valency increases from 1 to 4 and then decreases to zero in noble gases
Down a group, valency generally remains the same for elements in the same group
Elements in group 1 have valency 1, group 2 have valency 2, and so on
Transition metals often exhibit variable valency due to similar energies of (n-1)d and ns orbitals
Valency helps in predicting the chemical behavior of elements and their compounds

keyTerms.meaning: The electrons in the outermost shell of an atom that participate in chemical bonding
The number of electrons an atom can lose, gain, or share to form chemical bonds
The ability of some elements, especially transition metals, to exhibit more than one valency
Atoms tend to gain, lose, or share electrons to achieve a stable configuration with 8 valence electrons

sections.trick: Remember valency trend with '1-4-0' pattern - valency increases from 1 to 4 across a period, then drops to 0 in noble gases.
sections.examPointer: Questions on valency are common for 2-3 marks. You may be asked to determine valency of elements, explain the trend across periods and down groups, or discuss variable valency in transition metals.

sections.heading: Periodic Properties - Metallic Character
sections.para: Metallic character refers to the tendency of an element to lose electrons and form positive ions. It decreases across a period from left to right and increases down a group. This is because atomic size decreases across a period, making it harder for atoms to lose electrons. Down a group, atomic size increases, making it easier for atoms to lose electrons. For example, in period 3, sodium is the most metallic and chlorine is the least metallic. In group 17, fluorine is the least metallic and astatine is the most metallic. Elements on the left side of the periodic table are metals, those on the right are non-metals, and those in the middle are metalloids. The division between metals and non-metals is along the zigzag line starting from boron to astatine.
points: Metallic character is the tendency of an element to lose electrons and form positive ions
Metallic character decreases across a period from left to right due to decreasing atomic size
Metallic character increases down a group due to increasing atomic size
Elements on the left side of the periodic table are metals, those on the right are non-metals
The division between metals and non-metals is along the zigzag line from boron to astatine
Metalloids have properties intermediate between metals and non-metals

keyTerms.meaning: Elements that typically lose electrons to form positive ions, have high electrical and thermal conductivity, and are malleable and ductile
Elements that typically gain electrons to form negative ions, are poor conductors of heat and electricity, and are brittle
Elements that have properties intermediate between metals and non-metals, like silicon and germanium

sections.trick: Remember metallic character trend with 'L to R decreases, T to B increases' - Left to Right across a period, metallic character decreases; Top to Bottom down a group, metallic character increases.
sections.examPointer: Questions on metallic character are common for 2-3 marks. You may be asked to explain the trend, compare metallic character of given elements, or identify metals, non-metals, and metalloids in the periodic table.

sections.heading: Periodic Properties - Non-metallic Character
sections.para: Non-metallic character refers to the tendency of an element to gain electrons and form negative ions. It increases across a period from left to right and decreases down a group. This is because atomic size decreases across a period, making it easier for atoms to gain electrons. Down a group, atomic size increases, making it harder for atoms to gain electrons. For example, in period 2, lithium has the least non-metallic character and fluorine has the most. In group 16, oxygen has the most non-metallic character and polonium has the least. Non-metals are generally found on the right side of the periodic table, with hydrogen being an exception. The reactivity of non-metals decreases down a group, which is the opposite trend to metals. For example, fluorine is more reactive than chlorine, which is more reactive than bromine, and so on.
points: Non-metallic character is the tendency of an element to gain electrons and form negative ions
Non-metallic character increases across a period from left to right due to decreasing atomic size
Non-metallic character decreases down a group due to increasing atomic size
Non-metals are generally found on the right side of the periodic table
The reactivity of non-metals decreases down a group, opposite to the trend in metals
Hydrogen is an exception as it is a non-metal but is placed on the left side of the periodic table

keyTerms.meaning: Elements that typically gain electrons to form negative ions, are poor conductors of heat and electricity, and are brittle
The ability of an atom to attract shared electrons in a chemical bond, higher in non-metals
The tendency of an element to undergo chemical reactions, higher in more reactive elements
Substances that accept electrons in redox reactions, typically non-metals

sections.trick: Remember non-metallic character trend with 'L to R increases, T to B decreases' - Left to Right across a period, non-metallic character increases; Top to Bottom down a group, non-metallic character decreases.
sections.examPointer: Questions on non-metallic character are common for 2-3 marks. You may be asked to explain the trend, compare non-metallic character of given elements, or discuss the reactivity of non-metals.

sections.heading: Periodic Properties - Electronegativity
sections.para: Electronegativity is the ability of an atom to attract shared electrons in a chemical bond. It increases across a period from left to right and decreases down a group. This is because atomic size decreases across a period, making it easier for atoms to attract electrons. Down a group, atomic size increases, making it harder for atoms to attract electrons. For example, in period 2, lithium has the lowest electronegativity and fluorine has the highest. In group 17, fluorine has the highest electronegativity and astatine has the lowest. Electronegativity values are usually measured on the Pauling scale, where fluorine is assigned the highest value of 4.0. The difference in electronegativity between two atoms determines the nature of the bond they form - a large difference results in ionic bonding, while a small difference results in covalent bonding.
points: Electronegativity is the ability of an atom to attract shared electrons in a chemical bond
Electronegativity increases across a period from left to right due to decreasing atomic size
Electronegativity decreases down a group due to increasing atomic size
Electronegativity values are measured on the Pauling scale, with fluorine assigned 4.0
The difference in electronegativity determines bond type - large difference for ionic, small for covalent
Noble gases have very low or zero electronegativity as they have complete valence shells

keyTerms.meaning: The ability of an atom to attract shared electrons in a chemical bond
A scale for measuring electronegativity where fluorine is assigned the highest value of 4.0
The uneven distribution of electrons in a covalent bond due to difference in electronegativity
The degree to which a bond has ionic character due to electronegativity difference

sections.trick: Remember electronegativity trend with 'L to R increases, T to B decreases' - Left to Right across a period, electronegativity increases; Top to Bottom down a group, electronegativity decreases.
sections.examPointer: Questions on electronegativity are common for 2-3 marks. You may be asked to explain the trend, compare electronegativity values of given elements, or discuss its relationship with bond type.

sections.heading: Importance of Periodic Classification
sections.para: The periodic classification of elements is of great importance in chemistry. It helps in systematizing and learning the properties of elements and their compounds. The periodic table allows scientists to predict the properties of undiscovered elements and their compounds. It helps in understanding the relationship between the electronic configuration and chemical properties of elements. The periodic table is useful in studying the trends in physical and chemical properties of elements, which helps in explaining chemical bonding and molecular structure. It also helps in identifying similarities and differences between elements, which is useful in developing new materials and compounds. The periodic table is a fundamental tool in chemistry that continues to evolve as new elements are discovered and new theories are developed.
points: The periodic table systematizes and organizes the properties of elements and their compounds
It helps in predicting the properties of undiscovered elements and their compounds
It establishes relationships between electronic configuration and chemical properties
The periodic table helps in studying trends in physical and chemical properties
It aids in understanding chemical bonding and molecular structure
The periodic table continues to evolve as new elements are discovered and theories are developed

The ability to forecast properties of undiscovered elements based on periodic trends

boardQuestions.question: Explain the types of reactions with examples. What is a redox reaction?
boardQuestions.answer: There are several types of chemical reactions: 1) Combination reactions: Two or more substances combine to form a single product. Example: 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO. 2) Decomposition reactions: A single compound breaks down into two or more substances. Example: 2H2O -> 2H2 + O2. 3) Displacement reactions: A more reactive element displaces a less reactive element from its compound. Example: Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu. 4) Double displacement reactions: Two compounds exchange ions to form two new compounds. Example: AgNO3 + NaCl -> AgCl + NaNO3. A redox reaction involves the transfer of electrons between species. It consists of oxidation (loss of electrons) and reduction (gain of electrons). Example: Zn + Cu2+ -> Zn2+ + Cu, where Zn is oxidized and Cu2+ is reduced.

boardQuestions.question: Write the chemical properties of acids and bases. Give two examples of each.
boardQuestions.answer: Chemical properties of acids: 1) Acids turn blue litmus paper red. 2) Acids react with metals to produce hydrogen gas. Example: 2HCl + Zn -> ZnCl2 + H2. 3) Acids react with carbonates to produce CO2. Example: 2HCl + CaCO3 -> CaCl2 + H2O + CO2. Chemical properties of bases: 1) Bases turn red litmus paper blue. 2) Bases react with acids to form salt and water (neutralization). Example: NaOH + HCl -> NaCl + H2O. 3) Bases react with non-metallic oxides to form salt and water. Example: 2NaOH + CO2 -> Na2CO3 + H2O.

boardQuestions.question: What is corrosion? How can it be prevented?
boardQuestions.answer: Corrosion is the gradual destruction of materials (usually metals) by chemical reactions with their environment. For example, iron rusts when exposed to oxygen and moisture. Prevention methods: 1) Galvanization: Coating iron with a layer of zinc. 2) Painting: Applying a protective paint layer to prevent contact with air and moisture. 3) Alloying: Mixing iron with other metals to make it less reactive, like stainless steel. 4) Oiling or greasing: Creating a barrier to prevent oxygen and water contact. 5) Sacrificial protection: Attaching a more reactive metal (like magnesium) to the iron, which corrodes instead.

boardQuestions.question: Explain the pH scale and its importance. What is the pH of (a) pure water, (b) lemon juice?
boardQuestions.answer: The pH scale measures the acidity or basicity of a solution, ranging from 0 to 14. pH < 7 indicates acidic, pH = 7 is neutral, and pH > 7 is basic. The pH is calculated as pH = -log[H+], where [H+] is the hydrogen ion concentration. Importance: 1) Determines the suitability of water for various purposes. 2) Controls chemical reactions in industrial processes. 3) Essential for biological processes. (a) Pure water has pH 7 (neutral). (b) Lemon juice is acidic with pH around 2-3 due to citric acid content.

boardQuestions.question: Describe the preparation and properties of washing soda. What is its chemical formula?
boardQuestions.answer: Washing soda is prepared by the Solvay process or from sodium carbonate. It is obtained by heating sodium carbonate (soda ash) with water under pressure: Na2CO3 + H2O -> Na2CO3·10H2O. Chemical formula: Na2CO3·10H2O. Properties: 1) It is a white crystalline solid. 2) It is soluble in water and gives a strongly alkaline solution. 3) It is used as a water softener and cleaning agent. 4) It decomposes on heating to form soda ash and steam. 5) It reacts with acids to produce CO2. Example: Na2CO3 + 2HCl -> 2NaCl + H2O + CO2.

boardQuestions.question: Explain the reactivity series with examples. How can it be used to predict displacement reactions?
boardQuestions.answer: The reactivity series arranges metals in order of decreasing reactivity. Most reactive: K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, C, Zn, Fe, Sn, Pb, H, Cu, Ag, Au, Pt. Least reactive. Examples: Potassium reacts vigorously with cold water, while copper does not react even with steam. The reactivity series can predict displacement reactions: A more reactive metal can displace a less reactive metal from its salt solution. Example: Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu (zinc displaces copper). However, Cu cannot displace Zn from ZnSO2. Similarly, hydrogen can displace less reactive metals from their acids: Zn + H2SO4 -> ZnSO4 + H2, but copper does not react with dilute H2SO4.

boardQuestions.question: What is metallurgy? Describe the extraction of iron from its ore.
boardQuestions.answer: Metallurgy is the process of extracting metals from their ores and refining them for use. The extraction of iron from its ore (haematite, Fe2O3) involves several steps: 1) Concentration: The ore is crushed and concentrated by gravity separation or froth flotation. 2) Calcination: The concentrated ore is heated strongly in excess air to remove impurities as volatile oxides. 3) Reduction: The calcined ore is mixed with coke and limestone and heated in a blast furnace. The reactions are: C + O2 -> CO2 (combustion of coke), CO2 + C -> 2CO (producer gas), Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2 (reduction of iron oxide). Limestone decomposes: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2, and CaO reacts with silica impurities: CaO + SiO2 -> CaSiO3 (slag). Molten iron collects at the bottom and is tapped off.

boardQuestions.question: Explain the process of corrosion in iron and its prevention methods.
boardQuestions.answer: Corrosion in iron (rusting) is an electrochemical process that requires oxygen, water, and an electrolyte. The process involves: 1) At the anode: Fe -> Fe2+ + 2e- (oxidation). 2) At the cathode: O2 + 2H2O + 4e- -> 4OH- (reduction). 3) Formation of rust: Fe2+ + 2OH- -> Fe(OH)2, which further oxidizes to Fe2O3·xH2O (rust). Prevention methods: 1) Galvanization: Coating with zinc, which acts as a sacrificial anode. 2) Painting or oiling: Creates a barrier against oxygen and moisture. 3) Alloying: Making stainless steel by adding chromium. 4) Cathodic protection: Connecting a more reactive metal (like magnesium) to the iron structure.

boardQuestions.question: What is covalent bonding? Explain with examples.
boardQuestions.answer: Covalent bonding is a type of chemical bonding where atoms share electron pairs to achieve stable electron configurations. It occurs between non-metals. Examples: 1) Hydrogen molecule (H2): Each H atom shares 1 electron to form H-H bond. 2) Water (H2O): Oxygen shares electrons with two hydrogen atoms. 3) Methane (CH4): Carbon shares electrons with four hydrogen atoms. The shared electrons are attracted to both nuclei, holding the atoms together. Covalent bonds can be single (sharing 1 pair), double (sharing 2 pairs), or triple (sharing 3 pairs) bonds.

boardQuestions.question: Describe the properties and uses of ethanol and ethanoic acid.
boardQuestions.answer: Ethanol (C2H5OH): Properties: 1) Colorless liquid with characteristic odor. 2) Miscible with water in all proportions. 3) Burns with blue flame. 4) Undergoes fermentation. Uses: 1) As a solvent in paints and medicines. 2) As a fuel (biofuel). 3) In alcoholic beverages. 4) In antiseptic solutions. Ethanoic acid (CH3COOH): Properties: 1) Colorless liquid with vinegar-like smell. 2) Weak acid (pH 2-3). 3) Turns blue litmus red. 4) Forms esters with alcohols. Uses: 1) As vinegar in food. 2) In manufacture of plastics and dyes. 3) In making aspirin. 4) As a laboratory reagent.
